explain.title: Nutrition and nutrients
explain.body: Nutrition means the processes in which food is prepared or obtained and converted into body substances for growth and energy. Nutrients are the substances required by organism for energy, growth, repair, and maintenance.

explain.title: Mineral nutrients
explain.body: Mineral nutrients are special chemical elements absorbed from soil that are essential for plants to grow. Plants need these materials, in addition to the materials used in photosynthesis, to make other biomolecules.

explain.title: Two groups of minerals
explain.body: The minerals which are required in larger quantities are called macronutrients, for example carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, potassium, nitrogen, sulphur, calcium, and magnesium. The minerals which are required in lower quantities are called micronutrients, for example iron, molybdenum, boron, copper, manganese, zinc, chlorine, and nickel.

explain.title: Nitrogen and magnesium
explain.body: Nitrogen is a necessary part of proteins, enzymes, nucleic acids and chlorophyll. Roots absorb nitrogen in the form of nitrates. Magnesium is part of chlorophyll and activates many plant enzymes; roots absorb it in ionic form (Mg²⁺).

explain.title: Chlorosis
explain.body: A shortage of nitrogen or magnesium can cause chlorophyll to become insufficient and leaves to turn yellow. This yellowing is called chlorosis. The plant moves nitrogen or magnesium from older to younger leaves, so yellowing is seen in old leaves first.

mistakes: Do not swap the definitions: macronutrients are needed in larger quantities; micronutrients are needed in lower quantities.
Do not say that nitrogen is absorbed as magnesium ions; the section says roots absorb nitrogen as nitrates and magnesium as Mg²⁺.
Do not describe magnesium as only an enzyme activator; it is also a component of chlorophyll.
Use chlorosis for yellowing due to insufficient chlorophyll, not as the name for a mineral nutrient.

yourTurn.question: Explain the internal structure of root and describe the uptake of salt and water by root.
solution: The epidermis is the outermost covering of the root and is a single layer of cells.
Many epidermal cells have root hairs that extend into the spaces among soil particles.
Root hairs have a large surface area and are in direct contact with soil water.
Root hairs take in more salts by active transport.
Water moves from soil to root hairs by osmosis because the soil water has a lower concentration of salts than the root hairs.
Water with dissolved salts moves from the root hairs to the other cells of the epidermis, then through the cortex, endodermis and pericycle.
Water from the pericycle moves into the root xylem, from where it is transported to the xylem of the stem.

explain.title: The transport tissues
explain.body: In all land plants except mosses and liverworts, xylem and phloem carry materials. Xylem transports water and salts, while phloem transports food.

explain.title: Passive transport
explain.body: Passive Transport: It is the movement of ions or molecules across cell membrane from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. This movement does not require energy. Diffusion and osmosis are examples of passive transport.

explain.title: Active transport
explain.body: Active Transport: It is the movement of ions or molecules across cell membrane from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration, using energy. Root hairs take in more salts by active transport.

explain.title: Osmosis
explain.body: Osmosis: It is the movement of water molecules through a semi-permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration. This movement does not require energy. In the root, water moves from soil into root hairs by osmosis.

explain.title: The route through a root
explain.body: Root hairs take in water and salts from the soil. Water passes through the epidermis and cortex to the endodermis, then to the pericycle and into the xylem.

Do not say salts enter root hairs by osmosis; the section says salts enter by active transport.
Do not say water enters root hairs by active transport; it enters by osmosis.
Do not leave out the route through cortex, endodermis and pericycle in a long answer.
Do not stop the route at the pericycle; state that water moves into the xylem.

steps.why: Potassium uptake raises the solute concentration in the guard cells.
steps.text: During daytime, guard cells take in potassium ions from surrounding cells by active transport.

example.question: Describe the events involved in the opening and closing of stomata.
example.answer: During daytime, potassium ions enter guard cells, water follows by osmosis and the turgid guard cells open the stoma. In the evening, potassium ions and water leave the guard cells; they lose turgor and the stoma closes.

explain.title: What transpiration means
explain.body: The loss of water in the form of vapours from plant surface is called transpiration. Water can leave through stomata in leaves, the cuticle on the leaf epidermis, or lenticels in the stems of some plants.

explain.title: How water vapour leaves a leaf
explain.body: Water moves from xylem into the cell walls of mesophyll cells. It evaporates from the moist walls into the leaf’s air spaces, then moves towards the stomata and passes into the outside air. Most transpiration occurs through stomata and is called stomatal transpiration.

explain.title: How stomata open and close
explain.body: Stomata open and close because the turgor pressure of their guard cells changes. In daytime, potassium ions enter guard cells by active transport; water follows by osmosis, making the guard cells turgid and opening the stoma. In the evening, potassium ions move back to epidermal cells and water leaves, so the guard cells lose turgor and the stoma closes.

explain.title: Why transpiration matters and what affects it
explain.body: Transpiration is a necessary evil: it creates a pull on water columns in the xylem, helping transport water and salts from roots to leaves. Higher temperature and wind increase transpiration, while higher humidity lowers it. Leaves with more surface area transpire more, and in most plants the lower leaf surface transpires more because it has more stomata.

mistakes: Do not say that guard cells open because water leaves them; water enters them by osmosis during daytime, making them turgid.
Do not reverse the evening events: potassium ions and water move out of guard cells, and the stoma closes.
Do not write that humidity increases transpiration; higher humidity lowers its rate.
Do not give only the effect of temperature or wind: include the reason given in the section.
Do not confuse transpiration with only stomatal water loss; water can also leave through the cuticle and lenticels.

writtenQuestions.text: Describe the mechanism of transport of water and salt in plants.
modelAnswer: Roots cannot push the absorbed water to the leaves of the plant.
Transpiration of water from leaf surfaces creates a pulling force called transpirational pull.
A continuous water column in xylem extends from leaves to stem and to roots.
Attraction among water molecules, the narrow diameter of xylem vessels and adhesion to xylem walls help create this continuous column.
When water moves up through the leaf xylem, it produces tension on the whole column, so the column is pulled upwards from roots towards leaves.
Dissolved salts are carried upwards with the water.

writtenQuestions.text: Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism
modelAnswer: At the source, sucrose enters the sieve tubes of phloem by active transport.
Companion cells provide energy for this active transport.
The higher solute concentration in sieve tubes causes water to enter from nearby xylem by osmosis.
Fluid pressure in sieve tubes increases at the source, and the food solution flows towards the sink.
At the sink, sucrose is actively unloaded from sieve tubes into the sink tissues.
Water moves by osmosis from sieve tubes into the xylem, reducing fluid pressure in sieve tubes.
Because fluid pressure is higher at the source than at the sink, food flows in bulk towards the sink.

explain.title: What is translocation?
explain.body: “We know that inside the plant body, food is transported from one part to the other through phloem tissue.” This movement of food is called translocation. In most plants, glucose is converted into sucrose for transport.

explain.title: Sources and sinks
explain.body: “The sources include photosynthetic tissues (e.g. mesophyll of leaves) and storage tissues (e.g. roots). Sinks include the sites of food utilization (e.g. growing tips of roots and stems) and the storage tissues.” A source supplies food; a sink uses or stores it.

explain.title: Pressure flow mechanism
explain.body: “The mechanism of the transport of food in plants is called pressure flow mechanism.” At the source, sucrose loading causes water to enter the sieve tubes by osmosis, raising fluid pressure.

explain.title: Food moves towards the sink
explain.body: “Due to higher fluid pressure at the source than the sink, food flows in bulk towards the sink.” At the sink, sucrose is unloaded and water moves into the xylem, lowering the pressure.

explain.title: Xylem and phloem differ
explain.body: “Xylem is a one-way passage for water and salts (from roots to leaves). Phloem is a two-way passage for food.” Food direction depends on supply and demand at sources and sinks.

yourTurn.question: Describe the process of gaseous exchange in plants
solution: Gaseous exchange in plants occurs through the body surface.
The epidermis of roots, stems and leaves allows gases to exchange between the inner cells and the environment; a thick cuticle over some parts also allows exchange.
In leaves and young stems, gases move in and out through stomata; inside the plant body, gases are exchanged between cells and air.
In woody stems, bark does not allow gaseous exchange, so special pores called lenticels allow exchange with the environment.
During daytime, leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen; at night, plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

explain.title: Gas exchange changes between day and night
explain.body: During the daytime, all plant cells carry out cellular respiration while green parts also carry out photosynthesis. In photosynthesis, they use carbon dioxide and release oxygen. At night, photosynthesis does not occur, but respiration continues: plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

explain.title: Plant surfaces allow gases to pass
explain.body: “In plants, the gaseous exchange between body and the environment occurs through the surface.” The epidermis of roots, stems and leaves allows exchange between inner cells and the environment. A thick cuticle over some parts also allows gas exchange.

explain.title: Stomata serve leaves and young stems
explain.body: “In leaves and young stems, the air moves in and out through the stomata present in epidermis.” Inside the plant body, gaseous exchange occurs between cells and air.

explain.title: Lenticels serve woody stems
explain.body: “In woody stems, the entire surface is covered by bark. Gaseous exchange cannot occur through bark.” Special pores in the bark, called lenticels, allow gaseous exchange with the environment.

mistakes: Do not say that photosynthesis continues at night; respiration continues, but there is no photosynthesis.

explain.title: Mineral nutrition
explain.body: Plants need mineral elements for growth and life processes. Macronutrients are needed in large amounts, while micronutrients are needed in small amounts. Nitrogen helps plants make amino acids and proteins; magnesium is needed for chlorophyll.

explain.title: Roots absorb water and minerals
explain.body: Root hairs provide a large surface area for absorption. Water enters root cells by osmosis, while mineral ions are absorbed mainly by active transport. The ions and water move through root tissues towards the xylem.

explain.title: Transpiration and stomata
explain.body: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from aerial parts of a plant. Guard cells regulate the stomatal pore. When guard cells take up water they become turgid and open the pore; when they lose water they become flaccid and close it.

explain.title: Transport through xylem and phloem

notes.title: Mineral Nutrition in Plants
notes.answer: Plants absorb mineral nutrients from soil. Macronutrients are needed in larger quantities, and micronutrients are needed in lower quantities. Nitrogen is a component of proteins and chlorophyll. Magnesium is a component of chlorophyll and activates many enzymes.
notes.explanation: Plants need mineral nutrients from the soil to make important substances and grow. Macronutrients are needed in large quantities, while micronutrients are needed in small quantities. Nitrogen is used to make proteins and chlorophyll; magnesium is part of chlorophyll.
notes.simple: Plants take useful minerals from the soil. They need some minerals a lot and others only a little.
examples: Potassium is a macronutrient because plants need it in larger quantities.
Iron is a micronutrient because plants need it in lower quantities.
steps: Classify a mineral by how much of it plants need.
If plants need it in larger quantities, it is a macronutrient.
If plants need it in lower quantities, it is a micronutrient.
Recall that nitrogen is a component of proteins and chlorophyll.
Recall that magnesium is a component of chlorophyll.
notes.checkQuestion: State one role of nitrogen and one role of magnesium in plants.
notes.checkAnswer: Nitrogen is needed for proteins and chlorophyll; magnesium is a component of chlorophyll and activates many enzymes.

notes.title: How roots take in water and salts
notes.answer: Root hairs absorb salts by active transport and water by osmosis. Water and dissolved salts then pass through the root to the xylem.
notes.explanation: Water and mineral salts enter the root mainly through root hairs. Root hairs take in salts by active transport, and water follows by osmosis. The water and dissolved salts then pass through the root towards the xylem.
notes.simple: Root hairs take in salts, and water moves in after them. The water and salts travel through the root to the xylem.
examples: Root hairs take salts in by active transport.
Water moves from soil into root hairs by osmosis.
steps: Root hairs touch the soil water and provide a large surface area.
Root hairs take in salts from the soil by active transport.
Water moves from soil into root hairs by osmosis.
Water and dissolved salts pass through the epidermis, cortex, endodermis and pericycle.
Water moves from the pericycle into the root xylem.
notes.checkQuestion: How do root hairs absorb salts and water from the soil?
notes.checkAnswer: Root hairs absorb salts by active transport; water enters by osmosis.

notes.title: Transpiration and stomata
notes.answer: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapours from the plant surface. It occurs through stomata, the cuticle and lenticels.
notes.explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant’s surface. Most water vapour leaves through stomata. Guard cells open or close the stomata by changing their turgor, and factors such as temperature, wind and humidity affect how quickly water is lost.
notes.simple: Plants lose water vapour, mostly through tiny openings in their leaves. Wind usually speeds up this loss; high humidity slows it down.
examples: On a windy day, moving air carries away humid air around leaves, so more water can evaporate.
When guard cells take in potassium ions, water enters them by osmosis and the stoma opens.
steps: Water moves from the xylem into the cell walls of mesophyll cells.
Water evaporates from the moist walls into the air spaces in the leaf.
Water vapours move towards the stomata and pass to the outside air.
During daytime, potassium ions enter guard cells, water follows by osmosis, and the guard cells become turgid so the stoma opens.
In the evening, potassium ions and water move out of guard cells; they lose turgor and the stoma closes.
notes.checkQuestion: Why does wind speed up transpiration?
notes.checkAnswer: Wind carries away humid air around the leaves, allowing more water to evaporate.

notes.title: How water moves upwards in plants
notes.answer: Transpirational pull is the pulling force created by transpiration from leaf surfaces; it pulls water upwards through the xylem.
notes.explanation: Water evaporating from leaf surfaces creates a pulling force called transpirational pull. This pull draws water upwards through the continuous water column in the xylem, from roots to leaves.
notes.simple: Leaves lose water, and that loss pulls more water up from the roots through the xylem.
examples: When mesophyll cells lose water, more water enters them from the xylem.
As water moves up through the leaf xylem, tension pulls the water column upwards through the stem and roots.
steps: Water is lost from the leaf surfaces by transpiration.
Mesophyll cells lose water, so more water enters them from the xylem.
The water column in the xylem is continuous from leaves through the stem to the roots.
Movement of water in the leaf xylem creates tension in the whole column.
This tension pulls the water column upwards.
notes.checkQuestion: What creates the pulling force that moves water upwards in a plant?
notes.checkAnswer: Transpiration from leaf surfaces creates the pull.

notes.title: How food moves through a plant
notes.answer: Food moves through phloem from a source to a sink because fluid pressure is higher at the source than at the sink.
notes.explanation: Food is transported through phloem. In most plants, it travels as sucrose from a source, where food is available, to a sink, where food is used or stored. Loading sucrose at the source draws water into the phloem and raises its pressure. At the sink, sucrose is unloaded and water leaves the phloem, lowering its pressure. This pressure difference drives the flow of food.
notes.simple: Think of food flowing through phloem from where it is supplied to where it is needed or stored. Water pressure helps push it along.
examples: A mesophyll cell in a leaf can be a source; a growing root tip can be a sink.
A root storing food can be a source when it supplies food, or a sink when it receives food for storage.
steps: At the source, sucrose is actively loaded into the sieve tubes.
Water enters the sieve tubes from nearby xylem by osmosis.
The fluid pressure rises at the source, pushing food solution towards the sink.
At the sink, sucrose is actively unloaded and water moves into the xylem by osmosis.
The pressure is lower at the sink, so food flows in bulk from the higher-pressure source towards it.
notes.checkQuestion: Why does food flow from the source towards the sink?
notes.checkAnswer: Food moves in phloem from higher pressure at the source towards lower pressure at the sink.

notes.title: Gaseous Exchange in Plants
notes.answer: Plants exchange gases through their surfaces. Leaves and young stems mainly use stomata, while woody stems use lenticels.
notes.explanation: Plants exchange gases with their environment through their surfaces. Leaves and young stems use stomata, while woody stems use lenticels because their bark does not allow gaseous exchange.
notes.simple: Plants exchange gases through openings or surfaces. In daylight, photosynthesis changes which gases leaves exchange with the environment; at night, respiration continues without photosynthesis.

notes.title: How Plants Excrete Wastes
notes.answer: Plants excrete gases through surfaces and stomata, extra water by transpiration or guttation, and other wastes by storing or excreting them.
notes.explanation: Plants get rid of extra gases, water and other metabolic wastes in different ways. They release gases through surfaces and stomata, remove water by transpiration or guttation, and may store or excrete other wastes.
notes.simple: Excretion is how a plant gets rid of substances it does not need. It can release them, store them, or keep them in leaves that later fall.
examples: Grass can release water droplets from the tips or edges of its leaves at night by guttation.
Rubber plants excrete latex, while keekar trees excrete gum.
steps: Plants release excess carbon dioxide and oxygen through their general surfaces and stomata.
Plants remove extra water by transpiration during the day or by guttation at night.
Plants may store wastes as harmless crystals or in leaves that later fall.
Some plants excrete wastes through special pores, such as latex, gum, resin or mucilage.
notes.checkQuestion: How is guttation different from dew formation?
notes.checkAnswer: Guttation is the release of water droplets through small pores at the tips or edges of leaves. Dew forms when water vapour in the air condenses on the leaf surface.

notes.title: How plants adjust to their habitats
notes.answer: There are four types based on habitat: mesophytes, hydrophytes, xerophytes, and halophytes.
notes.explanation: Plants adjust how they take up, keep, or lose water according to their habitat. For example, a cactus stores water in succulent organs, while a water lily removes extra water through stomata on its leaves.
notes.simple: Plants living in different places use different ways to manage water and salts.
examples: A cactus is a xerophyte with a succulent stem.
A water lily is a hydrophyte with broad floating leaves.
steps: Identify the plant's habitat: moderate, wet, very dry, or salty.
Match the habitat to the plant type: mesophyte, hydrophyte, xerophyte, or halophyte.
State the adaptation that helps the plant manage water or salts.
notes.checkAnswer: A halophyte absorbs salts to make its body hypertonic, so water does not move out of its cells.

notes.title: Plant physiology: uptake, transport and excretion
notes.answer: Water enters root cells by osmosis.
notes.explanation: Plants need mineral nutrients, water and gases to grow. Roots absorb water and mineral salts, xylem carries them upwards, and phloem transports food. Transpiration helps pull water through a plant, while plants also use several ways to remove or store wastes.
notes.simple: Roots take in water and minerals, leaves exchange gases and lose water vapour, and transport tissues move water and food around the plant.
examples: Root hairs increase the surface area for absorbing water and mineral salts.
On a windy day, moving air removes moist air from around leaves, so transpiration usually increases.
steps: Root hairs absorb water from the soil by osmosis and mineral salts by diffusion or active transport, depending on the salt and conditions.
Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral salts from roots towards the leaves.
Water evaporates from leaf surfaces and exits mainly through stomata; this loss is transpiration.
Transpiration creates a pull that helps draw water upwards through xylem.
Phloem transports dissolved food, mainly sucrose, from sources to sinks by pressure flow.

written.text: Describe the mechanism of transport of water and salt in plants.
modelAnswer: Roots cannot push the absorbed water to the leaves of the plant.
Transpiration of water from leaf surfaces creates a pulling force called transpirational pull.
A continuous water column in xylem extends from leaves to stem and to roots.
Attraction among water molecules, the narrow diameter of xylem vessels and adhesion to xylem walls help create this continuous column.
When water moves up through the leaf xylem, it produces tension on the whole column, so the column is pulled upwards from roots towards leaves.
Dissolved salts are carried upwards with the water.

written.text: Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism
modelAnswer: At the source, sucrose enters the sieve tubes of phloem by active transport.
Companion cells provide energy for this active transport.
The higher solute concentration in sieve tubes causes water to enter from nearby xylem by osmosis.
Fluid pressure in sieve tubes increases at the source, and the food solution flows towards the sink.
At the sink, sucrose is actively unloaded from sieve tubes into the sink tissues.
Water moves by osmosis from sieve tubes into the xylem, reducing fluid pressure in sieve tubes.
Because fluid pressure is higher at the source than at the sink, food flows in bulk towards the sink.

written.text: Q9.3. Describe temperature, wind and humidity as the factors affecting the rate of transpiration.
modelAnswer: Higher temperature generally increases transpiration because evaporation and diffusion of water vapour become faster.
Wind usually increases transpiration by carrying away moist air from around the leaves.
High humidity decreases transpiration because the air already contains much water vapour.
This reduces the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and the surrounding air.
Final answer: Higher temperature and wind usually increase transpiration, while high humidity decreases it.

modelAnswer: Root hairs absorb water from the soil by osmosis.
Mineral ions enter root hairs mainly by active transport.
Water and dissolved salts pass through the root tissues and enter the xylem.
They move upwards through xylem, helped by root pressure and the transpiration pull created by water loss from leaves.
Final answer: Water enters by osmosis and salts mainly by active transport; both are carried upwards in xylem.

written.text: Q9.5. Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism
modelAnswer: At the source, such as a leaf, sucrose is loaded into the phloem.
This lowers the water potential in the phloem, so water enters from nearby xylem by osmosis.
The entry of water raises the pressure in the phloem at the source.
Phloem sap moves down the pressure gradient towards a sink, where sucrose is unloaded for use or storage.
Water then moves out of the phloem, helping maintain the pressure difference between source and sink.
Final answer: Food moves in phloem from source to sink because water entry at the source creates a pressure gradient.

written.text: Q9.6. How do the plants excrete extra water and salts from their bodies?

Excess salts may be removed through roots or leaves.
Plants may store wastes in leaves, bark or other tissues that are later shed.
Some plants also excrete wastes in substances such as gums and latex.
Final answer: Extra water is removed by transpiration and guttation; salts and other wastes are released, stored or removed with shed tissues.

modelAnswer: Gaseous exchange in plants occurs mainly by diffusion.

During respiration, oxygen enters and carbon dioxide leaves.
Final answer: Plants exchange gases by diffusion through stomata and lenticels.

written.text: Q9.9. Explain osmotic adjustments in in hydrophytes, xerophytes and halophytes.
modelAnswer: Hydrophytes grow where water is abundant, so they generally need little osmotic adjustment to obtain water.
Xerophytes face water shortage; they can accumulate solutes in cells, lowering water potential and helping cells absorb or retain water.
Halophytes live in salty habitats, where the surrounding solution makes water uptake difficult.
They accumulate compatible solutes in their cytoplasm or store salts in vacuoles, helping maintain water uptake while limiting salt damage.
Final answer: Xerophytes and halophytes adjust cell solute concentrations to maintain water uptake; hydrophytes live where water is readily available.

written.text: Q9.1. Why do plants transpire more on a windy day compared to a humid one?

Final answer: Wind increases transpiration by removing moist air; humidity lowers it by reducing the water-vapour gradient.
